evaluated.name: DebtFundedWorkingCapitalBuildup
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(wcap, 1), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital accruals that are funded by an expanding debt-to-assets ratio signal balance-sheet pressure: receivables and inventory are being built with borrowed money rather than operating cash, raising both reversal risk and default risk.
evaluated.reasoning: DELTA(wcap,1)/at isolates the working-capital accrual channel, and the change in total leverage isolates the funding source, so their rank product is elevated only for firms that are simultaneously accrual-aggressive and levering up. The multiplicative form encodes a genuine conditional effect: working-capital buildup is far more likely to reverse (and to be forced to reverse) when it is externally, rather than internally, financed.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsSignedByFinancingDirection
evaluated.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), SIGN(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accrual anomaly is concentrated among net issuers and is muted or reversed among net distributors; the same accrual level carries opposite information depending on whether the firm is absorbing or returning capital.
evaluated.reasoning: SIGN of net external financing switches the accrual signal on for issuers (where accruals plausibly reflect earnings management ahead of a raise) and flips it for repurchasers/debt retirers, whose high accruals more often reflect genuine growth in a cash-rich firm. This is a state-dependent conditioning of a classic accrual measure rather than a mechanical blend, so its predictive slope should be sharper than unconditional accruals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PersistentAccrualFinancingYears
evaluated.expression: TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 0.01)), 5)
evaluated.hypothesis: Repeated years of simultaneously positive accruals and material net external financing identify a chronic, not transitory, gap between reported earnings and self-funding capacity, which is a stronger overvaluation signal than any single-year coincidence.
evaluated.reasoning: Each year contributes 1 only if the firm is both accrual-positive and a meaningful net capital raiser (>1% of assets), so the five-year sum is a persistence count of the joint state rather than a magnitude blend. Persistence matters economically because one-off issuance or a single accrual spike is often benign, whereas a firm structurally dependent on external funding while reporting non-cash earnings is far more likely to disappoint.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IssuanceWeightedAccrualAcceleration
evaluated.expression: MUL(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A year-over-year jump in the non-cash share of earnings is informative about earnings management only when the firm is concurrently absorbing outside capital; the same accrual increase in a self-funding or capital-returning firm carries little overvaluation content.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the Sloan accrual *level* with its first difference removes most of the standalone accrual-anomaly loading and isolates a fresh accrual spike, which is the object the earnings-management-around-financing story actually predicts; the cross-sectional rank of net external financing then acts as a continuous [0,1] conditioning weight that attenuates the accrual spike toward zero for repurchasers and debt retirers instead of double-counting them as in an additive blend. Because the weight is monotone and never negative, the signal is a pure interaction term rather than a re-labeling of two known main effects, and coverage stays high since both legs use standard annual items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsUnderRefinancingPressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, dltr), che), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Aggressive accruals are most dangerous when the firm faces near-term debt that must be rolled over and holds insufficient cash to cover it, because forced refinancing exposes the accrual-inflated earnings to lender scrutiny and often triggers dilutive issuance or asset sales.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the dividend/repurchase payout channel entirely, so the contaminating positive shareholder-yield effect that the critic flagged is absent; the financing leg is instead maturing obligations (short-term debt plus long-term debt reduction) net of the cash cushion, a balance-sheet-pressure variable with an unambiguously negative expected return relation. The rank product makes the signal top out only for firms that are simultaneously accrual-aggressive and liquidity-short against maturing debt, which is the joint stress state the economic story requires and which neither leg identifies alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PostIssuanceAccrualPersistence
evaluated.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RANK(LAG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc)), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that raised external equity in the prior year and still report high accruals in the current year are sustaining an inflated earnings picture after the raise, and their accruals should reverse more severely than those of comparable non-issuers.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing leg uses the clean-surplus residual (change in book equity less retained earnings, i.e., ΔCEQ − IB + DVC), a split- and stock-dividend-immune measure of externally raised equity, which directly answers the mechanical-noise objection to raw share-count growth. Lagging the issuance leg by one year imposes an explicit timing structure — accruals are evaluated *after* the capital raise — so the signal tests post-issuance earnings-quality persistence rather than restating the contemporaneous issuance anomaly, and the [0,1] rank weight prevents the interaction from flipping sign for capital-returning firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsInLeveredCapitalStructure
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: It is the stock of total obligations, not merely the maturity schedule, that converts accrual aggressiveness into realized underperformance: highly levered firms have the least slack to absorb an accrual reversal and the strongest incentive to manage earnings toward covenants.
evaluated.reasoning: Paired with Signal 1, this isolates a single design choice — near-term liquidity gap versus total leverage as the conditioning state — so the batch teaches us *which* balance-sheet-pressure variable carries the −6.9% alpha found in gen 0. Total liabilities over assets is nearly universally reported, giving the highest coverage of any conditioning leg tried so far, and it is not itself a strong standalone return predictor, so any spread must come from the interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ChronicExternalFundingWithAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that has depended on outside capital for three consecutive years is structurally unable to self-fund; current accrual aggressiveness in such a firm signals an earnings picture propped up to keep the funding window open, and predicts worse returns than the same accruals in a self-financing firm.
evaluated.reasoning: PersistentAccrualFinancingYears showed the persistence idea has content but its six-valued integer construction created massive ties, a degenerate FMB slope, and an unstable sort (fmb = −1.52 with sharpe = −0.99 and a sign-inconsistent alpha); replacing the indicator count with a continuous three-year cumulative funding flow removes the ties while keeping the chronic-dependence economics. The financing flow aggregates debt and clean-surplus equity, so it captures total external capital reliance rather than one market.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: JointOwnHistoryAccrualLeverageExtreme
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is a firm being simultaneously at the top of its *own* five-year history for both accrual aggressiveness and indebtedness — a regime shift in accounting and funding behavior — rather than its permanent cross-sectional level, which largely reflects industry and business-model characteristics.
evaluated.reasoning: Every prior proposal conditioned on cross-sectional ranks, which load on stable firm traits (capital intensity, industry leverage norms) already spanned by FF5 factors, plausibly explaining why alpha appeared without an FMB slope; within-firm time-series ranks difference those traits away and isolate the behavioral change. This is the batch's distinct-mechanism entry: it tests whether the accrual-financing interaction is a state-change phenomenon rather than a level phenomenon, and its answer will redirect the remaining generations either way.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithDebtMaturityShortening
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(dltt, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When creditors will only extend short-dated credit, a firm's funding mix shifts toward current debt; combined with aggressive accruals this reveals that informed lenders are discounting the reported earnings that equity investors are still taking at face value.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the equity-issuance channel entirely — the Bradshaw–Richardson–Sloan territory the critic identified — for debt *maturity composition*, which is not a published cross-sectional anomaly and captures a credit-market opinion about the borrower rather than an issuance quantity. Measuring the shift as the change in short-term debt over assets minus the change in long-term debt over assets keeps the leg defined for unlevered and lightly levered firms (no zero-debt denominator), so coverage stays at the balance-sheet level rather than collapsing to the cash-flow-statement sample.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtBurdenPerInternalResource
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm's true debt burden should be measured against the internal resources actually available to service it — the larger of its cash-backed (accrual-purged) earnings and its cash balance — so the ratio rises jointly when accruals hollow out earnings and when the debt stock is large relative to those resources.
evaluated.reasoning: The degeneracy objection is fixed by making the denominator a firm-specific maximum of two economically substitutable resources: cash-backed earnings (IB less balance-sheet total accruals) and the cash stock, so the accrual-hollowed group no longer collapses onto a single common scalar — a cash-rich, accrual-heavy firm and a cash-poor, accrual-heavy firm are correctly separated, which is exactly the joint content the previous version lost. Depreciation enters only as a third-level floor that binds for the rare firm with both non-positive cash earnings and no cash, and the construction uses only balance-sheet and income-statement primitives (no `wcap`, no cash-flow-statement items), with WINSOR at 1% keeping the Fama-MacBeth slope from being driven by a handful of small-denominator observations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: IndustryNeutralDebtBurdenPerCashEarnings
evaluated.expression: IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accrual-adjusted debt-burden effect is a firm-level financing-and-accounting-quality phenomenon, not a bet on capital-intensive, high-leverage industries; ranking within industry should retain the abnormal return.
evaluated.reasoning: Leverage and depreciation-heavy cash-earnings profiles are strongly industry-clustered, and industry tilts are partially spanned by the FF5 investment and profitability factors, so the archived alpha may be a static sector bet whose Sharpe was only −0.21 despite a −4.47 alpha t-stat. Pairing this with Signal 1 — identical construct, one ranked globally and one within industry — cleanly separates "cross-industry leverage tilt" from "within-industry accounting-quality-under-debt", and whichever survives tells us where to concentrate the remaining generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: StressedChronicExternalFinancier
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1)), RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The firms that should underperform most are those that are simultaneously carrying debt they cannot service from cash-backed earnings *and* have been repeatedly returning to capital markets for three years — stock stress and flow dependence together, not either alone.
evaluated.reasoning: This deliberately joins the archive's alpha channel (debt burden per internal resource, α=−5.5%) with its slope channel (three-year external funding, fmb=−3.53) using MIN, a strict conjunction whose high end requires both conditions and whose low end unambiguously means "neither stress present" — unlike a rank product, whose interior pools contradictory states and is the prime suspect for the family's flat slopes. If the flow leg's FF5-spanned component is what killed its alpha, conditioning it on the stress leg should restore abnormal return while retaining the monotone cross-sectional ordering.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DeterioratingDebtServiceCoverage
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What the market misprices is not the permanent level of debt relative to cash-backed earnings — a stable firm trait largely spanned by factor exposures — but a sharp within-year deterioration in that coverage, caused either by debt rising or by earnings turning accrual-hollow.
evaluated.reasoning: Instead of monotonically rescaling the archived level ratio, this differences it, converting a static capital-structure characteristic into a transition variable: a firm moves into the short leg only when its debt burden per unit of accrual-purged internal resource worsens this year. That is a substantively different economic claim (deterioration versus stress level), it removes the industry/business-model component that a level ratio carries and that FF5 partly spans, and because the change is roughly symmetric around zero it is far better behaved as a Fama-MacBeth regressor than the fat-tailed level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualDominatedEarningsWhileLevering
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), MAX(ABS(ib), dp)), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The danger sign is the share of reported profit that is accrual rather than cash — earnings that exist only on paper — occurring in a year when the firm is adding leverage, since both the reported profit and the new borrowing depend on that accounting holding up.
evaluated.reasoning: The indicator is removed entirely, which eliminates the artifact the critic identified (loss-makers assigned zero and thereby swept into the long leg); accrual intensity is instead scaled by the magnitude of reported earnings, floored at depreciation, so the measure is continuous and defined for every firm while still rising precisely when accruals dominate the profit line. Scaling accruals by earnings rather than by assets is also a genuinely different measurement of accounting quality from everything in the archive, which has uniformly used asset-scaled accruals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OpaqueAccrualsAmplifiedByLeverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at), 5)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose accruals swing unpredictably from year to year have low-information earnings; when such opacity sits on top of a large debt load, investors and creditors cannot distinguish a temporary shortfall from a solvency problem, and the equity carries mispriced tail risk.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the accrual-level-times-leverage form entirely and moves to a second moment: five-year accrual volatility is an earnings-quality/opacity construct (Dechow–Dichev in spirit) that is essentially uncorrelated with the accrual level, so the resulting signal is not a re-weighting of the archived AccrualsInLeveredCapitalStructure. The interaction is economically necessary rather than decorative: accrual noise is tolerable in an unlevered firm and destabilizing in a levered one, so neither leg alone should carry the effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PayerDividendCoverageGapWithLevering
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dvt, SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp))), dvt), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms that actually pay dividends, the fraction of the declared payout not covered by accrual-purged cash earnings measures how much of the distribution is being financed rather than earned; when that gap coincides with rising debt, the payout is being borrowed and its eventual cut is not priced.
evaluated.reasoning: Dividing the coverage gap by `dvt` itself makes the signal undefined for non-payers, so they drop out of the cross-section rather than being assigned zero and pooled into the long leg — the exact defect the critic flagged, fixed by construction rather than by an indicator multiplication. The restriction is economically intended, not a coverage patch: the payout-sustainability hypothesis is a statement about dividend payers, ranks are formed within that population, and the leverage-increase leg ensures the short leg contains only firms genuinely borrowing to defend the distribution.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ExternalFundsBurnedIntoWorkingCapital
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital raised and immediately consumed — external funding that does not show up as an increase in the cash balance — is qualitatively worse than capital raised and held, and worst of all when the absorbing use is a swelling working-capital position rather than productive investment.
evaluated.reasoning: Every prior financing leg measured the *amount* raised, which is why FF5's investment factor absorbed it; this leg measures the *fate* of the money (raised minus retained in cash), a disposition variable that is not a scaled investment characteristic and therefore has a better chance of surviving the CMA control. Conjoining it with the working-capital accrual identifies firms whose new outside money went into receivables and inventory — the classic soft-asset buildup that later reverses.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithOwnHistoryFinancingSurge
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: What is mispriced is not being a habitually capital-hungry firm — a stable trait the investment factor already prices — but raising an unusual amount of capital relative to the firm's own funding history while the accounting turns aggressive.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the targeted repair of the archive's clearest failure: ChronicExternalFundingWithAccruals ordered the cross-section correctly (fmb=−3.53) yet earned no alpha (t=−0.72), the signature of a characteristic spanned by CMA. Replacing the cross-sectional rank of cumulative financing with a within-firm five-year TS_RANK holds the accrual leg and operator structure fixed and changes only the benchmark against which financing is judged, so the comparison cleanly identifies whether within-firm financing surprise is the FF5-orthogonal part of the effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EquityForDebtSwapWithAggressiveAccruals
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc)), at), RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Substituting equity for debt — issuing shares while paying debt down — is a market-timing decision made when management believes the stock is dear; when it coincides with aggressive accruals, the "dearness" is partly manufactured accounting and the equity was sold to investors at an inflated price.
evaluated.reasoning: This measures financing *mix* rather than financing *quantity*, so a firm with zero net external funding still scores high if the composition swung from debt to equity, which makes the leg close to orthogonal to total investment and hence to CMA — the factor that neutralized the flow-based entries. The conjunction with accruals is essential to the story: an equity-for-debt swap by a firm with cash-backed earnings is prudent deleveraging, while the same swap by an accrual-heavy firm is opportunistic issuance.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsAtOwnDebtCapacityCeiling
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), TS_MAX(ADD(dltt, dlc), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm sitting at the maximum debt level of its own five-year history has exhausted the borrowing capacity its lenders have historically granted it; aggressive accruals in that state are dangerous because the inevitable reversal cannot be bridged with additional debt.
evaluated.reasoning: Cross-sectional leverage levels are industry- and business-model-determined and correlate with FF5-spanned traits, which is consistent with the industry-neutral version of the debt-burden signal losing 40% of its alpha; scaling current debt by the firm's own five-year maximum makes the conditioner scale-free and firm-relative, so a modestly levered firm at its personal ceiling counts as constrained while a permanently high-leverage utility does not. This is a capacity-exhaustion concept rather than a burden-level concept, which is the one untried variant of the stress channel that could deliver alpha without the static-characteristic loading.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ExternalShareOfCumulativeFundingSources
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), 3), MAX(TS_SUM(ADD(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp))), 3), TS_SUM(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is the *share* of a firm's three-year funding that came from outside investors rather than from cash-backed internal earnings; a firm approaching 100% external funding is one whose reported profits generate no self-financing capacity, which is precisely the accrual-plus-financing overvaluation archetype.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not an average of previously tested legs with arbitrary weights but a single accounting share in which accruals and financing are inseparable: the same dollar of accrual simultaneously reduces cash-backed earnings in the denominator and raises the external share, so the numerator and denominator cannot be decomposed into the archive's two legs. Being a bounded proportion rather than an unbounded stress ratio, it is well behaved as a Fama-MacBeth regressor — addressing the family's chronic null slope — while remaining distinct from a scaled investment characteristic because two firms with identical asset growth score very differently depending on the cash content of their earnings.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashBackedEarningsWithCapitalReturned
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The mirror image of the overvaluation archetype should be rewarded: firms whose earnings are cash-backed *and* which are simultaneously retiring debt and equity are financing themselves entirely from operations, a self-discipline configuration the market underprices.
evaluated.reasoning: The lag-timing idea is abandoned as the critic's point is correct — returns are already measured after the fiscal year — and replaced with a test of *which side of the spread* carries our repeated alpha, which the archive cannot answer because every entry has been sorted from the stressed corner. Note this is not the negative of any archived signal: MIN applied to negated ranks selects firms clean on *both* dimensions (a MAX-type conjunction on the original scale), a corner never isolated before, and if this long-side construct produces alpha we should build the remaining generations around capital-return discipline rather than around distress.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EquityFundedBurnWithWorkingCapitalAccruals
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc)), DELTA(che, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The overvaluation story is specifically about *equity* sold into an accrual-inflated earnings picture and immediately spent; debt-funded burn is a credit-risk phenomenon, while equity-funded burn is a mispricing phenomenon and should be the part that earns abnormal returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-3 winner pooled debt and clean-surplus equity in one funding leg, so we cannot tell whether we discovered a distress effect or an issuance-overvaluation effect; isolating the equity component while holding the accrual leg and operator fixed answers that directly. This matters for consolidation because the two readings imply different refinements — credit-stress conditioners versus issuance-timing conditioners — and we have five generations left to spend on the right one.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SoftAssetTiltOfExternallyFundedGrowth
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), DELTA(SUB(at, act), 1)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Where the raised money went matters as much as that it was spent: outside capital absorbed by receivables and inventory is far more reversal-prone than outside capital converted into productive long-lived assets, so the soft-versus-hard tilt of growth should sharpen the burn signal.
evaluated.reasoning: Non-current assets are recoverable as at − act, so working-capital accrual minus long-lived asset growth is a clean use-of-funds contrast that no archive entry has tested; it converts the accrual leg from "how much soft-asset buildup" into "how soft-asset-tilted the firm's investment was". This is the asset-side complement to Signal 2's source-side decomposition, and because a firm with large hard investment is deliberately down-weighted, the leg is less collinear with plain asset growth and hence less exposed to the CMA absorption that killed our early financing legs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UnderDepreciationWithExternalBurn
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp))))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Depreciation policy is an accrual choice: a firm charging an unusually low depreciation rate against its long-lived asset base relative to industry peers is deferring expense recognition, and doing so while consuming externally raised cash is the accounting-plus-funding combination that precedes write-downs.
evaluated.reasoning: Every accrual leg in the archive has been a working-capital or Sloan-style balance-sheet accrual; the depreciation rate is a structurally different earnings-quality lever, largely orthogonal to working-capital accruals, and it must be judged against industry peers because asset lives are technology-determined — hence the IND_ZSCORE rather than a raw rank. Pairing a new accounting-quality dimension with the funding leg we now trust is the cheapest way to learn whether the alpha is specific to soft-asset accruals or general to aggressive accounting.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BurnRelativeToCashRunway
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), MAX(che, dp)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The severity of consuming externally raised capital depends on the buffer behind it: a dollar of burn is trivial for a cash-rich firm and existential for one operating on a thin cash balance, so scaling the burn by the cash stock rather than by assets identifies the firms that must return to the market on someone else's terms.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than re-parameterizing the horizon — a question the archive already answered when three-year cumulation of the funding leg destroyed its alpha — this changes the *denominator* from size to liquidity buffer, converting the gen-3 winner's leg from a flow-intensity measure into a runway measure. Firms with identical asset-scaled burn are now sharply separated by how much cash stands behind it, which should concentrate the short leg in genuinely constrained firms and lift alpha, while the accrual leg is held fixed so the comparison is clean.

evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that suddenly consumes far more outside capital than its own recent three-year norm has changed funding regime, and that break — not the permanently capital-hungry business model that factor models already price — is what coincides with unrecognized accrual risk.
evaluated.reasoning: The coarseness objection is fixed by measuring own-history deviation as a continuous gap between the current burn rate and its three-year moving average, so nothing in the composite has five mass points and the MIN cannot be floored by a lumpy term. It is also not a remix of the archived TS_RANK signal: a within-firm rank says only "highest of five years", whereas the deviation says how far above its own norm the firm has moved, which is the quantity a regime-change hypothesis actually requires and which retains full cross-sectional resolution for the Fama-MacBeth slope.

evaluated.hypothesis: When the interest-bearing share of a firm's liabilities rises, costly market debt is replacing free supplier credit — evidence that trade creditors, who see order and payment behaviour before equity investors do, are pulling back; combined with a swelling soft-asset position this signals that the receivables and inventory on the balance sheet are of lower quality than reported.
evaluated.reasoning: The previous version's conditioner was wrong-signed because rising payables lower accruals and predict higher returns; inverting the framing to the *composition* of liabilities removes that contradiction, since a shift away from trade credit toward interest-bearing debt is unambiguously a tightening of the firm's cheapest funding source. Both legs now point the same way economically, the mechanism (informed-creditor withdrawal) is distinct from every burn- and leverage-based entry in the archive, and the leg uses only high-coverage balance-sheet primitives with `lt` as a stable denominator.

If the differenced version retains the −4.95-class slope, the effect is an accounting *choice*; if it collapses, the level version was proxying for asset composition and the final generations should keep the level form and control it differently.

evaluated.hypothesis: New borrowing that is large relative to the firm's stock of hard, pledgeable assets must be secured against receivables and inventory instead of plant; when that borrowing coincides with a swelling soft-asset position, the loan collateral and the accrual risk are the same assets, and a collection or obsolescence shortfall hits the lender and the equity simultaneously.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a recombination of two archived signals with a genuinely untested financing dimension — borrowing capacity measured against pledgeable collateral rather than against assets, earnings, cash or maturity — and it pairs naturally with the soft-asset accrual leg because the two describe the same assets from the creditor's and the accountant's side. Scaling new debt by net non-current assets (floored at depreciation) is scale-free and uses only high-coverage primitives, so the family's 0.11 coverage should be preserved.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DepreciationRateBelowOwnPeakWithBurn
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Conservatism erodes cumulatively: what matters is how far a firm's current effective depreciation rate sits below the most conservative rate it has itself applied in the last five years, regardless of whether that erosion arrived in one step or many.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a state variable, not another horizon of the same change variable — a firm whose rate fell sharply and then stabilized scores high here but scores zero on a one-year change and weakly on a trend, so the three constructions genuinely separate event, drift and accumulated position. The ratio to the firm's own five-year maximum is bounded in (0,1], which makes it well behaved as a Fama-MacBeth regressor and immune to the small-denominator leverage that afflicts raw rate changes.

evaluated.name: OwnPeakDeferralWithEquityCushionBurn
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5)))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), MAX(ceq, dp)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose effective depreciation rate has eroded far below its own historical peak, and which is consuming outside capital at a rate that is large relative to the shareholders' own capital cushion, combines the strongest available measure of accounting erosion with the strongest available measure of funding intensity.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are the best-performing versions of their respective dimensions discovered independently in gen 8 (erosion state: fmb −5.37, α −3.9%; equity-scaled burn: α −3.8%, t −4.23), and they were each tested against a *different* partner, so their combination is an untried cell rather than a reshuffle of an evaluated pair. The equity denominator embeds a leverage tilt that the asset denominator lacks, which should concentrate the short leg in firms where the burn genuinely threatens the residual claim.

evaluated.name: BurnPerPeakRestatedCashEarnings
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), MAX(SUB(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), SUB(MUL(TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5), SUB(at, act)), dp)), dp)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings should be restated at the most conservative depreciation rate the firm itself has applied in the last five years before asking how many dollars of outside capital each dollar of genuine internal cash generation had to support; the erosion of conservatism and the funding dependence then enter one continuous quantity.
evaluated.reasoning: The prior restatement ratio used only last year's depreciation charge as the benchmark (α=−3.1%, fmb=−4.49); replacing it with the five-year peak rate applied to the current asset base imports the erosion concept that just produced the archive's best signal, and does so in a full-support continuous form rather than a MIN conjunction whose long leg pools contradictory states. This is the batch's answer to the family's persistent slope-versus-alpha tension: continuous ratios have reliably delivered the strongest slopes, and this one now carries the winning accounting content.

evaluated.name: IndustryAdjustedOwnPeakDeferralWithBurn
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5))))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Whole industries let their effective depreciation rates drift down during capital-expenditure booms, so the firm-specific component of accumulated conservatism erosion — the part exceeding the contemporaneous industry move — is the accounting decision that carries information.
evaluated.reasoning: Industry-demeaning the *one-year change* raised the slope from −4.51 to −4.66 in gen 7 at a modest alpha cost, and the erosion state is more exposed to industry capex cycles than the change is because it accumulates them over five years, so the demeaning should matter more here. Together with Signal 1 and Signal 6 this completes a 2×2 design whose fourth cell is the existing champion, letting us attribute any final improvement to the accounting normalization, the funding normalization, or their interaction.

evaluated.name: OwnPeakDeferralWithCollateralScarceBorrowing
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5)))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Borrowing that is large relative to the firm's stock of pledgeable hard assets must be secured against soft assets or against the reported earnings themselves; when those earnings are supported by an eroded depreciation charge, lender and shareholder are relying on the same overstated numbers.
evaluated.reasoning: The collateral-scarcity leg delivered α=−3.3% (t=−2.84) in gen 8 when paired with the working-capital accrual, but it has never met the erosion state that now carries the family's alpha, and it is a genuinely different financing dimension from burn intensity, funding tenor and funding source. Both legs share the net non-current asset base as a scaling anchor, which makes the joint interpretation coherent: the same hard-asset stock that is too small to secure the new debt is also the base whose depreciation is being understated.

evaluated.name: ErodedConservatismWithSoftAssetsOverEquity
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, che), MAX(ceq, dp))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The exposure that matters may be a pair of *states* rather than flows: accumulated erosion of depreciation conservatism alongside a soft-asset stock that dwarfs the book equity available to absorb its write-down, with no requirement that anything dramatic happened in the current year.
evaluated.reasoning: Every signal in the archive has included at least one annual flow, yet the two alpha-richest non-flow constructions — the erosion state (α=−3.9%) and soft assets over the equity cushion (α=−3.4%, t=−3.61) — have never been combined, and a state-only signal would have far lower portfolio turnover than the flow-based family. The known risk is the slope: the soft-asset-over-equity leg had fmb=−1.08 on its own, so this tests explicitly whether the erosion state supplies enough cross-sectional ordering to rescue a stock-only construction.

evaluated.name: LiquidityCompositionBelowOwnPeakWithBurn
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(che, act), TS_MAX(RATIO(che, act), 5)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The cash share of current assets measures how much of a firm's reported liquidity is certain rather than dependent on collection and sale; a firm sitting far below the most cash-backed composition it has achieved in five years has quietly converted its liquidity into accrual-based claims, and doing so while consuming outside capital is the balance-sheet analogue of deferring depreciation.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than stacking two normalizations onto the same champion leg, this transfers the single most productive discovery of the search — distance from the firm's own five-year best, which lifted the depreciation lever from fmb −4.51 to −5.37 — onto an entirely different balance-sheet dimension, testing whether "accumulated erosion versus own peak" is a general property of accounting-quality variables or specific to depreciation policy. The corresponding one-year change of the same variable was the weakest quality leg in the archive (α=−1.9%, t=−2.28), so a strong result here would be attributable to the state framing rather than to the underlying ratio, which is exactly the inference the final generation should be able to draw.

considered.name: DebtFundedWorkingCapitalBuildup
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(wcap, 1), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Working-capital accruals that are funded by an expanding debt-to-assets ratio signal balance-sheet pressure: receivables and inventory are being built with borrowed money rather than operating cash, raising both reversal risk and default risk.
considered.reasoning: DELTA(wcap,1)/at isolates the working-capital accrual channel, and the change in total leverage isolates the funding source, so their rank product is elevated only for firms that are simultaneously accrual-aggressive and levering up. The multiplicative form encodes a genuine conditional effect: working-capital buildup is far more likely to reverse (and to be forced to reverse) when it is externally, rather than internally, financed.

considered.name: AccrualsSignedByFinancingDirection
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), SIGN(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr))))
considered.hypothesis: The accrual anomaly is concentrated among net issuers and is muted or reversed among net distributors; the same accrual level carries opposite information depending on whether the firm is absorbing or returning capital.
considered.reasoning: SIGN of net external financing switches the accrual signal on for issuers (where accruals plausibly reflect earnings management ahead of a raise) and flips it for repurchasers/debt retirers, whose high accruals more often reflect genuine growth in a cash-rich firm. This is a state-dependent conditioning of a classic accrual measure rather than a mechanical blend, so its predictive slope should be sharper than unconditional accruals.

considered.name: PersistentAccrualFinancingYears
considered.expression: TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 0.01)), 5)
considered.hypothesis: Repeated years of simultaneously positive accruals and material net external financing identify a chronic, not transitory, gap between reported earnings and self-funding capacity, which is a stronger overvaluation signal than any single-year coincidence.
considered.reasoning: Each year contributes 1 only if the firm is both accrual-positive and a meaningful net capital raiser (>1% of assets), so the five-year sum is a persistence count of the joint state rather than a magnitude blend. Persistence matters economically because one-off issuance or a single accrual spike is often benign, whereas a firm structurally dependent on external funding while reporting non-cash earnings is far more likely to disappoint.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IssuanceWeightedAccrualAcceleration
considered.expression: MUL(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A year-over-year jump in the non-cash share of earnings is informative about earnings management only when the firm is concurrently absorbing outside capital; the same accrual increase in a self-funding or capital-returning firm carries little overvaluation content.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the Sloan accrual *level* with its first difference removes most of the standalone accrual-anomaly loading and isolates a fresh accrual spike, which is the object the earnings-management-around-financing story actually predicts; the cross-sectional rank of net external financing then acts as a continuous [0,1] conditioning weight that attenuates the accrual spike toward zero for repurchasers and debt retirers instead of double-counting them as in an additive blend. Because the weight is monotone and never negative, the signal is a pure interaction term rather than a re-labeling of two known main effects, and coverage stays high since both legs use standard annual items.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsUnderRefinancingPressure
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, dltr), che), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Aggressive accruals are most dangerous when the firm faces near-term debt that must be rolled over and holds insufficient cash to cover it, because forced refinancing exposes the accrual-inflated earnings to lender scrutiny and often triggers dilutive issuance or asset sales.
considered.reasoning: This drops the dividend/repurchase payout channel entirely, so the contaminating positive shareholder-yield effect that the critic flagged is absent; the financing leg is instead maturing obligations (short-term debt plus long-term debt reduction) net of the cash cushion, a balance-sheet-pressure variable with an unambiguously negative expected return relation. The rank product makes the signal top out only for firms that are simultaneously accrual-aggressive and liquidity-short against maturing debt, which is the joint stress state the economic story requires and which neither leg identifies alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PostIssuanceAccrualPersistence
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RANK(LAG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc)), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that raised external equity in the prior year and still report high accruals in the current year are sustaining an inflated earnings picture after the raise, and their accruals should reverse more severely than those of comparable non-issuers.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg uses the clean-surplus residual (change in book equity less retained earnings, i.e., ΔCEQ − IB + DVC), a split- and stock-dividend-immune measure of externally raised equity, which directly answers the mechanical-noise objection to raw share-count growth. Lagging the issuance leg by one year imposes an explicit timing structure — accruals are evaluated *after* the capital raise — so the signal tests post-issuance earnings-quality persistence rather than restating the contemporaneous issuance anomaly, and the [0,1] rank weight prevents the interaction from flipping sign for capital-returning firms.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsInLeveredCapitalStructure
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
considered.hypothesis: It is the stock of total obligations, not merely the maturity schedule, that converts accrual aggressiveness into realized underperformance: highly levered firms have the least slack to absorb an accrual reversal and the strongest incentive to manage earnings toward covenants.
considered.reasoning: Paired with Signal 1, this isolates a single design choice — near-term liquidity gap versus total leverage as the conditioning state — so the batch teaches us *which* balance-sheet-pressure variable carries the −6.9% alpha found in gen 0. Total liabilities over assets is nearly universally reported, giving the highest coverage of any conditioning leg tried so far, and it is not itself a strong standalone return predictor, so any spread must come from the interaction.

considered.name: ChronicExternalFundingWithAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that has depended on outside capital for three consecutive years is structurally unable to self-fund; current accrual aggressiveness in such a firm signals an earnings picture propped up to keep the funding window open, and predicts worse returns than the same accruals in a self-financing firm.
considered.reasoning: PersistentAccrualFinancingYears showed the persistence idea has content but its six-valued integer construction created massive ties, a degenerate FMB slope, and an unstable sort (fmb = −1.52 with sharpe = −0.99 and a sign-inconsistent alpha); replacing the indicator count with a continuous three-year cumulative funding flow removes the ties while keeping the chronic-dependence economics. The financing flow aggregates debt and clean-surplus equity, so it captures total external capital reliance rather than one market.

considered.name: JointOwnHistoryAccrualLeverageExtreme
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 5))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is a firm being simultaneously at the top of its *own* five-year history for both accrual aggressiveness and indebtedness — a regime shift in accounting and funding behavior — rather than its permanent cross-sectional level, which largely reflects industry and business-model characteristics.
considered.reasoning: Every prior proposal conditioned on cross-sectional ranks, which load on stable firm traits (capital intensity, industry leverage norms) already spanned by FF5 factors, plausibly explaining why alpha appeared without an FMB slope; within-firm time-series ranks difference those traits away and isolate the behavioral change. This is the batch's distinct-mechanism entry: it tests whether the accrual-financing interaction is a state-change phenomenon rather than a level phenomenon, and its answer will redirect the remaining generations either way.

considered.name: WeakestLinkAccrualLiquidityDeterioration
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What predicts underperformance is not a static funding gap but a *widening* one: firms whose near-term debt is growing faster than their cash while they simultaneously book aggressive accruals are deteriorating on both the accounting and the funding dimension at once.
considered.reasoning: Two substantive changes address the archive-duplication and the alpha-without-slope puzzle: the financing leg becomes a flow (the year-over-year change in short-term-debt-minus-cash), so the signal identifies a deteriorating state rather than a permanent capital-structure trait already spanned by FF5 loadings, and the aggregator becomes MIN rather than MUL. MIN is a strict conjunctive operator — it is high only when *both* legs are high and its low end unambiguously means "at least one dimension is fine" — which removes the mixed "high accrual / low pressure" pooling that made the archived rank product non-monotone in its interior and plausibly flattened its Fama-MacBeth slope to −0.27 despite a −4.24 alpha t-stat.

considered.name: AccrualsWithDebtMaturityShortening
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at)), RANK(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(dltt, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: When creditors will only extend short-dated credit, a firm's funding mix shifts toward current debt; combined with aggressive accruals this reveals that informed lenders are discounting the reported earnings that equity investors are still taking at face value.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the equity-issuance channel entirely — the Bradshaw–Richardson–Sloan territory the critic identified — for debt *maturity composition*, which is not a published cross-sectional anomaly and captures a credit-market opinion about the borrower rather than an issuance quantity. Measuring the shift as the change in short-term debt over assets minus the change in long-term debt over assets keeps the leg defined for unlevered and lightly levered firms (no zero-debt denominator), so coverage stays at the balance-sheet level rather than collapsing to the cash-flow-statement sample.

considered.name: DebtBurdenPerInternalResource
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: A firm's true debt burden should be measured against the internal resources actually available to service it — the larger of its cash-backed (accrual-purged) earnings and its cash balance — so the ratio rises jointly when accruals hollow out earnings and when the debt stock is large relative to those resources.
considered.reasoning: The degeneracy objection is fixed by making the denominator a firm-specific maximum of two economically substitutable resources: cash-backed earnings (IB less balance-sheet total accruals) and the cash stock, so the accrual-hollowed group no longer collapses onto a single common scalar — a cash-rich, accrual-heavy firm and a cash-poor, accrual-heavy firm are correctly separated, which is exactly the joint content the previous version lost. Depreciation enters only as a third-level floor that binds for the rare firm with both non-positive cash earnings and no cash, and the construction uses only balance-sheet and income-statement primitives (no `wcap`, no cash-flow-statement items), with WINSOR at 1% keeping the Fama-MacBeth slope from being driven by a handful of small-denominator observations.

considered.name: IndustryNeutralDebtBurdenPerCashEarnings
considered.expression: IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The accrual-adjusted debt-burden effect is a firm-level financing-and-accounting-quality phenomenon, not a bet on capital-intensive, high-leverage industries; ranking within industry should retain the abnormal return.
considered.reasoning: Leverage and depreciation-heavy cash-earnings profiles are strongly industry-clustered, and industry tilts are partially spanned by the FF5 investment and profitability factors, so the archived alpha may be a static sector bet whose Sharpe was only −0.21 despite a −4.47 alpha t-stat. Pairing this with Signal 1 — identical construct, one ranked globally and one within industry — cleanly separates "cross-industry leverage tilt" from "within-industry accounting-quality-under-debt", and whichever survives tells us where to concentrate the remaining generations.

considered.name: StressedChronicExternalFinancier
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1)), RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: The firms that should underperform most are those that are simultaneously carrying debt they cannot service from cash-backed earnings *and* have been repeatedly returning to capital markets for three years — stock stress and flow dependence together, not either alone.
considered.reasoning: This deliberately joins the archive's alpha channel (debt burden per internal resource, α=−5.5%) with its slope channel (three-year external funding, fmb=−3.53) using MIN, a strict conjunction whose high end requires both conditions and whose low end unambiguously means "neither stress present" — unlike a rank product, whose interior pools contradictory states and is the prime suspect for the family's flat slopes. If the flow leg's FF5-spanned component is what killed its alpha, conditioning it on the stress leg should restore abnormal return while retaining the monotone cross-sectional ordering.

considered.name: DeterioratingDebtServiceCoverage
considered.expression: WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), MAX(MAX(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), che), dp)), 1), 1)
considered.hypothesis: What the market misprices is not the permanent level of debt relative to cash-backed earnings — a stable firm trait largely spanned by factor exposures — but a sharp within-year deterioration in that coverage, caused either by debt rising or by earnings turning accrual-hollow.
considered.reasoning: Instead of monotonically rescaling the archived level ratio, this differences it, converting a static capital-structure characteristic into a transition variable: a firm moves into the short leg only when its debt burden per unit of accrual-purged internal resource worsens this year. That is a substantively different economic claim (deterioration versus stress level), it removes the industry/business-model component that a level ratio carries and that FF5 partly spans, and because the change is roughly symmetric around zero it is far better behaved as a Fama-MacBeth regressor than the fat-tailed level.

considered.name: AccrualDominatedEarningsWhileLevering
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), MAX(ABS(ib), dp)), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The danger sign is the share of reported profit that is accrual rather than cash — earnings that exist only on paper — occurring in a year when the firm is adding leverage, since both the reported profit and the new borrowing depend on that accounting holding up.
considered.reasoning: The indicator is removed entirely, which eliminates the artifact the critic identified (loss-makers assigned zero and thereby swept into the long leg); accrual intensity is instead scaled by the magnitude of reported earnings, floored at depreciation, so the measure is continuous and defined for every firm while still rising precisely when accruals dominate the profit line. Scaling accruals by earnings rather than by assets is also a genuinely different measurement of accounting quality from everything in the archive, which has uniformly used asset-scaled accruals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OpaqueAccrualsAmplifiedByLeverage
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp), at), 5)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose accruals swing unpredictably from year to year have low-information earnings; when such opacity sits on top of a large debt load, investors and creditors cannot distinguish a temporary shortfall from a solvency problem, and the equity carries mispriced tail risk.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the accrual-level-times-leverage form entirely and moves to a second moment: five-year accrual volatility is an earnings-quality/opacity construct (Dechow–Dichev in spirit) that is essentially uncorrelated with the accrual level, so the resulting signal is not a re-weighting of the archived AccrualsInLeveredCapitalStructure. The interaction is economically necessary rather than decorative: accrual noise is tolerable in an unlevered firm and destabilizing in a levered one, so neither leg alone should carry the effect.

considered.name: PayerDividendCoverageGapWithLevering
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dvt, SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp))), dvt), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms that actually pay dividends, the fraction of the declared payout not covered by accrual-purged cash earnings measures how much of the distribution is being financed rather than earned; when that gap coincides with rising debt, the payout is being borrowed and its eventual cut is not priced.
considered.reasoning: Dividing the coverage gap by `dvt` itself makes the signal undefined for non-payers, so they drop out of the cross-section rather than being assigned zero and pooled into the long leg — the exact defect the critic flagged, fixed by construction rather than by an indicator multiplication. The restriction is economically intended, not a coverage patch: the payout-sustainability hypothesis is a statement about dividend payers, ranks are formed within that population, and the leverage-increase leg ensures the short leg contains only firms genuinely borrowing to defend the distribution.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExternalFundsBurnedIntoWorkingCapital

considered.hypothesis: Managers choose which margin to manage — current-asset recognition or long-lived-asset expense deferral — so aggressiveness should be scored as elevation on *either* lever, and that index, not any single lever, is what should be conditioned on external cash consumption.
considered.reasoning: This is not the three-way intersection rejected earlier: the two accounting levers are pooled into an index inside which a firm aggressive on one margin still qualifies, and only that index is intersected with burn, so the extreme decile is not thinned by requiring both. Re-ranking the SUMRANK output puts the index on the same [0,1] scale as the burn rank, which is necessary for the MIN to be meaningful, and the design tests whether the two levers are substitutes (index wins) or complements (single-lever champion wins).

considered.name: EquityBurnPerRestatedCashEarnings
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc)), DELTA(che, 1)), MAX(SUB(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), SUB(MAX(dp, LAG(dp, 1)), dp)), dp)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: Equity raised and consumed per dollar of depreciation-restated cash earnings is the sharpest single expression of the overvaluation story: shares are sold on earnings that were flattered by expense deferral and the proceeds do not stay in the firm.
considered.reasoning: The two strongest continuous constructions can be combined without intersecting ranks — the equity-only numerator produced the archive's best slope (−5.02 in MIN form) while the restated denominator produced the best continuous ratio (−4.49 / −3.1%) — and unlike a MIN conjunction this keeps full cross-sectional support. The risk is the known equity/debt trade-off (equity sourcing sharpened the slope but cost alpha), so this proposal is explicitly a test of whether the restated denominator can restore the alpha that the equity-only numerator gives up.

considered.name: DeferralMaterialityToEarningsWithBurn
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(LAG(dp, 1), dp), MAX(ABS(ib), dp))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: What makes an expense deferral worth doing is its effect on the reported earnings number, so the right measure is the dollar reduction in the depreciation charge scaled by the magnitude of reported income — a small charge reduction can be decisive for a marginally profitable firm and irrelevant for a highly profitable one.
considered.reasoning: The loss-funding partition is dropped because the critic is right that netting asset growth out of the burn reconstructs a profitability bet through the balance-sheet identity; this replacement instead changes the *normalization* of the accounting lever from the asset base to the earnings base, which is an economic materiality concept rather than a rate concept and is therefore not a monotone re-expression of the champion's leg. It is continuous in both directions — a rising charge scores negative, a falling charge positive — so there is no mass point at zero and full cross-sectional support is retained for the slope.

considered.name: StraddledBurnWindowWithDepreciationCut
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(MAX(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at), LAG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at), 1))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Capital raised near a fiscal year-end is typically consumed in the following year, so a firm's burn episode straddles the annual reporting boundary; classifying a firm as burning if it burned in *either* of the last two years captures the episode regardless of where the year-end fell.
considered.reasoning: The two-sided spread is abandoned because the algebra is correct — differencing mirror-corner conjunctions collapses to an additive combination — and it is replaced with a measurement fix for a real timing artifact rather than another aggregation experiment. Taking the maximum of the current and lagged burn rates is not a horizon average like the three-year cumulation that previously destroyed alpha: it preserves the intensity of the single worst year while removing the arbitrary dependence on fiscal-year alignment, so the short leg should be cleaner without becoming a chronic-financing characteristic.

considered.name: HabitualDeferralWithExternalBurn
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 1)), 0), 5)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A single depreciation-rate decline can be an accident of asset mix, but a firm that has cut its effective depreciation rate in four or five of the last five years is running a policy of systematic expense deferral, and doing so while consuming outside capital marks earnings that have been managed habitually rather than once.
considered.reasoning: The beginning-of-year scaling is dropped as the critic correctly identifies it as a near-monotone reparameterization; this replacement instead asks a different question about the same lever — how *habitual* the choice is, which is robust to the magnitude outliers and single-year capex lumpiness that both the change and trend versions inherit. The count is deliberately paired with MUL rather than MIN so the coarse six-valued leg weights the continuous burn rank instead of flooring it, which is the specific lumpiness failure diagnosed for the earlier TS_RANK conjunction.

considered.name: BurnAgainstEquityCushionWithDeferral
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 1))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), MAX(ceq, dp)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: From the shareholder's standpoint the relevant intensity is capital consumed per dollar of *their* capital, not per dollar of total assets: an identical burn is far more dilutive and far more likely to force a rescue financing when the book equity cushion behind it is thin.
considered.reasoning: Every burn leg to date has been scaled by assets, cash, or cash earnings; scaling by book equity introduces a leverage tilt into the intensity measure, which is economically motivated — the same dollar burned by a highly levered firm consumes a larger share of the residual claim — and connects the family's most robust leg to the loss-absorption idea that earned α=−3.4% as a stock measure. It is a different economic normalization, not a monotone rescaling, because leverage varies enormously at any given asset-scaled burn rate.

considered.name: WorstMarginAggressivenessWithBurn
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(MAX(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 1))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Managers manage the margin that is easiest for them, so a firm should be judged by its *most* aggressive accounting choice rather than by the average across margins; extremity on one lever is the signal, and moderation on the other should not dilute it.
considered.reasoning: The gen-7 index averaged the two levers via SUMRANK and matched but did not beat the single-lever champion, which is exactly what one expects if the levers are substitutes and averaging pulls single-margin offenders toward the middle; the MAX aggregator makes the substitutes logic explicit and is the complementary aggregation experiment to the accepted index, so the pair identifies whether aggressiveness is best measured as an average or as a maximum.

considered.name: DeferralAgainstCreditorTenorTightening
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 1))), RANK(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(dltt, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: When management is stretching asset lives to support reported earnings while lenders are simultaneously shortening the maturity of the credit they extend, the two informed parties are moving in opposite directions — and the lenders are usually right.
considered.reasoning: The tenor leg produced a strong slope (−3.82) but weak alpha (−1.7%) when paired with the burn leg, and it has never been paired with the accounting lever that carries the family's alpha, so this tests whether creditor behaviour substitutes for the burn as the financing-side conditioner. It is also the batch's cleanest divergence story — accounting optimism versus credit-market caution — and its high-coverage construction (0.129 for the tenor leg) may lift the family's usable panel.

considered.name: BenchmarkedDepreciationShortfallWithBurn
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MUL(MA(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 3), SUB(at, act)), dp), at)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is the *dollars of depreciation expense a firm avoided* relative to what its own three-year policy applied to its current asset base would have charged; that shortfall, expressed as a share of assets, is the amount by which reported earnings were inflated, and it matters most in a firm consuming outside capital.
considered.reasoning: This is not a cardinal-versus-ordinal restatement: it builds an explicit counterfactual depreciation charge from the firm's own historical rate applied to today's asset base, so asset growth is handled inside the benchmark rather than left as a confound, and the output is a dollar shortfall scaled by assets rather than a rate change. It also fixes the small-denominator objection directly — asset-light firms have a tiny (at − act), so their benchmark shortfall is mechanically near zero rather than explosively large, meaning the short leg is populated by firms where the deferral is materially large in dollars.

considered.name: DebtRaisedBeyondHardCollateral
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), at)))
considered.hypothesis: New borrowing that is large relative to the firm's stock of hard, pledgeable assets must be secured against receivables and inventory instead of plant; when that borrowing coincides with a swelling soft-asset position, the loan collateral and the accrual risk are the same assets, and a collection or obsolescence shortfall hits the lender and the equity simultaneously.
considered.reasoning: This replaces a recombination of two archived signals with a genuinely untested financing dimension — borrowing capacity measured against pledgeable collateral rather than against assets, earnings, cash or maturity — and it pairs naturally with the soft-asset accrual leg because the two describe the same assets from the creditor's and the accountant's side. Scaling new debt by net non-current assets (floored at depreciation) is scale-free and uses only high-coverage primitives, so the family's 0.11 coverage should be preserved.

considered.name: DepreciationRateBelowOwnPeakWithBurn
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Conservatism erodes cumulatively: what matters is how far a firm's current effective depreciation rate sits below the most conservative rate it has itself applied in the last five years, regardless of whether that erosion arrived in one step or many.
considered.reasoning: This is a state variable, not another horizon of the same change variable — a firm whose rate fell sharply and then stabilized scores high here but scores zero on a one-year change and weakly on a trend, so the three constructions genuinely separate event, drift and accumulated position. The ratio to the firm's own five-year maximum is bounded in (0,1], which makes it well behaved as a Fama-MacBeth regressor and immune to the small-denominator leverage that afflicts raw rate changes.

considered.name: OwnPeakDeferralWithEquityCushionBurn
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5)))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), MAX(ceq, dp)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose effective depreciation rate has eroded far below its own historical peak, and which is consuming outside capital at a rate that is large relative to the shareholders' own capital cushion, combines the strongest available measure of accounting erosion with the strongest available measure of funding intensity.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are the best-performing versions of their respective dimensions discovered independently in gen 8 (erosion state: fmb −5.37, α −3.9%; equity-scaled burn: α −3.8%, t −4.23), and they were each tested against a *different* partner, so their combination is an untried cell rather than a reshuffle of an evaluated pair. The equity denominator embeds a leverage tilt that the asset denominator lacks, which should concentrate the short leg in firms where the burn genuinely threatens the residual claim.

considered.name: BurnPerPeakRestatedCashEarnings
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), MAX(SUB(SUB(ib, SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1)), DELTA(txp, 1))), dp)), SUB(MUL(TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5), SUB(at, act)), dp)), dp)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: Earnings should be restated at the most conservative depreciation rate the firm itself has applied in the last five years before asking how many dollars of outside capital each dollar of genuine internal cash generation had to support; the erosion of conservatism and the funding dependence then enter one continuous quantity.
considered.reasoning: The prior restatement ratio used only last year's depreciation charge as the benchmark (α=−3.1%, fmb=−4.49); replacing it with the five-year peak rate applied to the current asset base imports the erosion concept that just produced the archive's best signal, and does so in a full-support continuous form rather than a MIN conjunction whose long leg pools contradictory states. This is the batch's answer to the family's persistent slope-versus-alpha tension: continuous ratios have reliably delivered the strongest slopes, and this one now carries the winning accounting content.

considered.name: IndustryAdjustedOwnPeakDeferralWithBurn
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), TS_MAX(RATIO(dp, MAX(SUB(at, act), dp)), 5))))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), DELTA(che, 1)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Whole industries let their effective depreciation rates drift down during capital-expenditure booms, so the firm-specific component of accumulated conservatism erosion — the part exceeding the contemporaneous industry move — is the accounting decision that carries information.
considered.reasoning: Industry-demeaning the *one-year change* raised the slope from −4.51 to −4.66 in gen 7 at a modest alpha cost, and the erosion state is more exposed to industry capex cycles than the change is because it accumulates them over five years, so the demeaning should matter more here. Together with Signal 1 and Signal 6 this completes a 2×2 design whose fourth cell is the existing champion, letting us attribute any final improvement to the accounting normalization, the funding normalization, or their interaction.
